The Horror of a Russian Victory in Ukraine for Africa
text_paragraph_1: As Ukraine enters a new and terrifying phase of the Russian invasion of its territory, the cost of war is mounting for both countries in lives and economic development.
text_paragraph_2: At stake is Ukraine’s right to exist as a sovereign, independent nation. But the stakes are much higher than that. The central question is whether or not the world can accept a reversal of the democratic gains of the 20th century and return to a feudal system where elites rule, rights are trampled, and might is right. Ironically, a return to a 19th-century world of power politics is being spearheaded by Russia in Ukraine, the former displaying acute schizophrenia in being a permanent Security Council member of the United Nations, and (like China) calling for an overhaul of the global system. A case of having your cake and eating your neighbour’s slice too.
text_paragraph_3: At the heart of the Ukraine war is a clash of values. On the one side is an open democratic society with a free press, freedom of expression, a vocal civil society, and the entrenchment of democratic rights. It may be messy, but it’s a democracy, where people protest, openly criticise, and speculate.

text_paragraph_1: Esoumaila Diallo, only 19 years old, is scrambling to fill the hole left when his mother, Fatou Traore, was detained by ICE on September 24, and then deported to Sierra Leone, a country she had never set foot in. Diallo lives with his parents in Iowa City, Iowa, and has three little brothers, the youngest of whom is three years old. His mother’s sudden and unexpected arrest and deportation caused him to miss so much school that he withdrew from his current semester at Kirkwood Community College, though he plans to go back. “I had to step up and at least try to take over her role, which I can’t,” he says. “I’m definitely trying my best with my other siblings, taking care of the house, chores, and stuff like that. But it’s really, really hard.”
text_paragraph_2: Traore’s arrest has touched off outrage in her Iowa City community, where she works as a custodian at the University of Iowa Hospitals and Clinics. Originally from Côte d’Ivoire, she was granted a withholding of removal in 2011. “To get withholding of removal you have to show there’s at least a 50% chance that you’ll be persecuted in your home country,” explains Alma Leonie David, an immigration attorney who has been in touch with Traore but is not her lawyer. “What’s happening now is that people who’ve lived here in the U.S. for decades, have families, they own houses, they have jobs, they have community, they built their whole life here, thinking they were safe, now the U.S. is saying, ‘Well, actually, we will deport you to a third country.’”
text_paragraph_3: Diallo says his mother was detained after dropping off one of his brothers at early morning soccer practice, and then going to her sister’s house to take her to work. When he found out, he says, “I fly over there. I’m running as fast as I can to see what’s going on. But when I got there, unfortunately, it was too late. My mom was already gone with whoever took her.”

text_paragraph_1: The global economy is expanding at a steady pace, yet governments are losing the financial flexibility needed to protect it. An artificial intelligence investment boom is helping offset energy disruptions, but mounting public debt, higher borrowing costs and renewed inflationary pressures are leaving policymakers with increasingly difficult choices.
text_paragraph_2: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva delivered this warning in Bangkok, outlining an economic landscape where technological progress is accelerating faster than countries' capacity to manage its financial consequences. Global growth is projected at 3.1% in 2026, unchanged from the IMF's October 2025 forecast, but the stability of that headline figure conceals deepening economic divisions.
text_paragraph_3: The uncomfortable reality is that resilience today does not necessarily translate into preparedness for tomorrow. Countries are simultaneously financing technological transformation, absorbing geopolitical disruptions and servicing accumulated debt, while the financial buffers needed to withstand another shock are becoming harder to rebuild.

text_paragraph_1: Ethiopie : au Tigré, une administration intérimaire mise en place par le gouvernement fédéral Une administration intérimaire au Tigré, région en proie aux combats depuis plusieurs semaines et qui était dirigée jusque-là par les rebelles du Front de libération du peuple du Tigré (TPLF), est mise en place, a annoncé le bureau du premier ministre éthiopien, Abiy Ahmed sur Facebook, vendredi 16 octobre. Cette nouvelle administration, qui devra en particulier « créer un climat politique stable pour organiser des élections libres et transparentes », gouvernera cette région septentrionale de l’Ethiopie « pour les six prochains mois ». Le Tigré échappait depuis plusieurs mois au contrôle du gouvernement fédéral. La région, qui n’a pas participé aux dernières élections fédérales organisées le 1er juin, était dirigée par le TPLF. Ce parti non reconnu par Addis-Abeba a formé une alliance à la fin de fin septembre avec plusieurs groupes armés pour « renverser » le gouvernement d’Abiy Ahmed et s’est rapproché de l’Erythrée voisine, qui entretient des relations exécrables avec l’Ethiopie. text_paragraph_2: Somalie : le présidentielle et les législatives annoncées pour 2027 Les autorités somaliennes ont annoncé la tenue d’élections législatives et présidentielle en 2027, malgré l’aggravation des divisions politiques et les inquiétudes liées à l’instabilité du pays. Selon un communiqué de la Commission électorale, les législatives se dérouleront le 15 avril, suivies de l’élection présidentielle le 15 mai. Le calendrier électoral intervient alors que le mandat du président Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, élu en 2022, a pris fin plus tôt cette année. Son gouvernement a instauré une période de transition en mai, malgré un accord conclu avec l’opposition sur l’organisation des élections. Au cœur du différend figure une réforme constitutionnelle adoptée par le Parlement, qui redéfinit le cadre électoral et prolonge le calendrier du scrutin. Le chef de l’État estime que cette modification lui accorde une année supplémentaire à la présidence. Les partis d’opposition, qui ont boycotté le vote, contestent ces changements. La Commission électorale justifie la date de la présidentielle par une disposition fixant à cinq ans la durée du mandat présidentiel à compter de la prestation de serment. Cette interprétation ne met toutefois pas fin aux tensions entre le pouvoir central et ses adversaires, notamment les dirigeants régionaux, qui dénoncent une concentration des pouvoirs. Africanews avec AFP
text_paragraph_3: Le conflit de pouvoir dans le Sud-Ouest somalien à son paroxysme Les conflits s’intensifient en Somalie entre les autorités régionales et le gouvernement fédéral. Jeudi, des forces fidèles à l’ancien président de l’État du Sud-Ouest, Abdelaziz Hassan Mohamed, également connu sous le nom de « Laftagareen », ont pris le contrôle de la ville stratégique de Buurhakaba, située dans la région de Bay. Selon des responsables, de violents combats ont opposé ces forces à des troupes alignées sur le gouvernement fédéral et placées sous le commandement de Sheikh Aden Mohamed Nur Madobe. Les affrontements ont éclaté tôt jeudi à Buurhakaba. Des habitants ont fait état de tirs nourris et d’explosions, alors que les forces de Laftagareen attaquaient des positions tenues par les troupes fédérales et les forces régionales soutenant Madobe. Selon des informations locales, des combattants fidèles à l’ancien dirigeant régional ont ensuite pénétré dans plusieurs quartiers de la ville. Cette prise de contrôle marque une nouvelle escalade dans la lutte pour le pouvoir au sein de l’État du Sud-Ouest. Ces derniers jours, les forces alliées à Laftagareen s’étaient déjà emparées de Qansahdhere, un autre district de la région de Bay. APA

title: Opinion| A date is not democracy: Will South Sudan’s long-awaited elections deliver?
text_paragraph_1: South Sudan’s electoral debate risks confusing visible activity with meaningful readiness. Training sessions, registration materials, political meetings, and diplomatic visits can demonstrate progress. They cannot, on their own, guarantee that citizens will participate safely, candidates will compete fairly, or disputed results will be resolved peacefully. When these fundamentals receive less attention than public declarations of preparedness, an election can approach on the calendar while remaining distant in practice.
text_paragraph_2: The country’s long-awaited elections are scheduled for 22 December 2026. Whether they will take place cannot responsibly be answered with certainty. The stronger question is whether the remaining preparations can produce a credible electoral process within the available time. South Sudanese citizens deserve evidence of readiness, alongside assurances that their right to choose their leaders will finally be respected.
text_paragraph_3: There is evidence of preparation. On 2 September, the National Elections Commission reported training officials from the ten states and three administrative areas in voter registration. Such capacity building is essential. Its practical value, however, depends on whether trained personnel subsequently reach communities with adequate materials, funding, supervision and clear instructions. A successful workshop is one step towards registration; it is not evidence that nationwide registration has been completed.

text_paragraph_1: Today, 13 October 2026, the UN General Assembly (UNGA) elected Brazil, Burundi, Dominican Republic, Germany, Ghana, Ireland, Japan, Jordan, Kuwait, Nepal, Nigeria, Republic of Moldova, Ukraine, Uruguay and Zambia to the Human Rights Council (HRC) for the 2027-2029 term. With their election, 23 of the Council’s 47 members in 2027 will be “Friends of the Responsibility to Protect (R2P)” – states that have either appointed a Focal Point for R2P and/or joined the Group of Friends of R2P in New York and Geneva.
text_paragraph_2: Following these ‘clean slate’ elections, newly elected members of the HRC have an opportunity to strengthen the Council’s credibility and advance principled leadership in atrocity prevention. Membership in the HRC carries the obligation, set forth in UNGA Resolution 60/251 , to uphold the highest standards of human rights and to fully cooperate with the Council’s mechanisms and procedures. The re-election of Burundi therefore raises serious concerns about the Council’s credibility. Burundi has a documented history of atrocity crimes, and serious human rights violations continue in a climate of widespread impunity. No meaningful structural reforms have been implemented to address long-standing concerns related to human rights, governance, justice and the rule of law. The government of Burundi has also consistently failed to cooperate with the HRC’s mechanisms and has voted against resolutions addressing some of the world’s gravest human rights crises, including in Sudan , Ukraine , South Sudan , Belarus and Eritrea .
text_paragraph_3: Nevertheless, the new composition of the HRC presents a fresh chance to reinforce the Council’s essential role in preventing atrocities and protecting populations at risk, particularly as several members have already demonstrated strong commitments to this goal. text_paragraph_1: The government should invest in Flexible Open and Distance Education (FODE) to help upgrade the current elementary teacher workforce. FODE is an alternative pathway within PNG's national education system, allowing students to complete Grades 7–12 outside the conventional school environment — and offering teachers with only Grade 10 qualifications the same route to finishing their own secondary education. Students follow the national curriculum, complete assignments, and sit the equivalent of formal national school examinations. FODE is delivered through two mechanisms. The first is government-operated centres established by the Department of Education and provincial administrations, which have struggled with weak coordination, delayed materials, limited student support, inadequate infrastructure, and shortages of qualified teaching staff.
text_paragraph_2: The second is Registered Study Centres, which can be operated by churches, missions, community organisations, NGOs, and other approved providers. The Kokoda Track Foundation currently operates 24 registered FODE centres across six provinces. Its model offers flexible learning with full-time teachers, wrap-around student support, outreach patrols, digital tablets with offline content, solar-powered infrastructure, and active community engagement. A recent study found that this level of support directly improved student participation and retention.
text_paragraph_3: PNG's Infrastructure Tax Credit Scheme allows eligible resource companies to fund approved public infrastructure in exchange for credits. Companies such as Ok Tedi, Barrick, Newcrest, and ExxonMobil have supported the construction of classrooms and teacher housing, school upgrades, and training facilities. text_paragraph_1: An estimated 645 million people face hunger in the world. When market disruptions occur, they reverberate far beyond an immediate conflict zone. Right now, the global food market faces the impact of Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine, the war in the Middle East and the incoming El Nino. While everyone is affected, the most vulnerable countries, communities and persons are the least able to absorb another shock to food prices and supplies.
text_paragraph_2: Russia’s continued attacks on Ukraine – targeting its ports, shipping lanes, warehouses, inland logistics and agricultural infrastructure – are no longer just a war far away. Russia is systematically strangling Ukraine’s ability to feed the world. By targeting ports, shipping lanes, and agricultural infrastructure. it is weaponising hunger against millions in Africa, Asia, and the Middle East.

Congo-Kinshasa: DRC - Children, Disproportionately Affected Yet Left Behind in the Current Ebola Outbreak Response
text_paragraph_1: Children are paying a devastating price in the Ebola outbreak unfolding in northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). While children face a higher risk of death from Ebola than adults, they also represent a significant proportion of those affected by the current outbreak. According to Epicentre, MSF’s epidemiological research centre, nearly one in four confirmed Ebola cases in North Kivu is a child. Médecins sans Frontières (MSF) is deeply concerned by the disproportionate impact of the disease on children and calls for more attention to their specific vulnerabilities in both the medical and research response.
text_paragraph_2: While Ebola remains a deadly disease for all age groups, the youngest children face the highest risk of death. In North Kivu, children have been particularly affected by the current outbreak: 24% of confirmed cases are among children under five years of age, compared with 13% in Ituri, while infants under one year old account for 13% of cases, compared with 6% in Ituri. At the Ebola Treatment Centre (ETC) in Butembo, North Kivu, MSF teams have observed that the case fatality rate among children was particularly high. Between June and September 2026, 24 out of 30 children—most of whom under the age of five—died from the Bundibugyo virus in this ETC alone. The rapid progression of the disease in communities and limited access to specialised care at the health facility level are contributing to such alarmingly high fatality rates.
text_paragraph_3: “Primary health facilities often lack the specialized expertise, equipment, and infection prevention and control measures needed to identify and safely manage suspected cases,” explains Stéphanie Hoffmann, project coordinator for MSF in Butembo. “Most of the paediatric cases admitted in our ETC in Butembo, North Kivu, over the summer, had already been hospitalised for other illnesses in several facilities during the days or weeks before their admission. Their family members did not have Ebola themselves, and it is highly likely that these children contracted the disease inside healthcare facilities.” Strengthening infection prevention and control (IPC) measures in health facilities, ensuring the availability of personal protective equipment (PPE), and reinforcing the training of healthcare workers in non-Ebola health centres across at-risk areas are critical to maintaining essential services while preventing healthcare-associated transmission.

Disturbing Signals from The Gambia
text_paragraph_1: Something is brewing in The Gambia, our fellow West African country. Ordinarily, it looks like a simple, routine banking regulation exercise which should not worry any observer, but I fear there may be more to it — and Nigerians may be at the receiving end yet again. I hope I am proved wrong at the end of the day, but I want to raise my voice and draw the attention of the Nigerian authorities to it before whispers turn into shouts and push comes to shove. We must remember that for years, Nigerian immigrants suffered resentment in South Africa until the xenophobic attacks exploded. Also, Ghana has been hurting the interests of Nigerian businesses while, at the same time, smiling with us.
text_paragraph_2: On September 16, 2026, the Central Bank of The Gambia (CBG) sent a letter titled “Directive on the Recruitment of Non-Gambian Staff” to the MDs of all banks. It was signed by the second deputy governor, Dr Paul J. Mendy, who, I understand, was trained by the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN). It followed a meeting with bank chiefs on August 27, 2026, which, I heard, ended abruptly and resulted in the directive. The CBG, in its directive, said its industry study found that banks employ “a relatively high number of non-Gambians… in addition to recognised expatriate staff”. It said this breaches the Labour Act 2023 and Guideline 9 of its Management and Technical Services Agreement Guidelines.
text_paragraph_3: All banks are to replace their existing non-Gambian staff with “suitably qualified Gambian nationals”. The deadline is December 31, 2026 — about 15 weeks after the letter was issued. This has been well reported. The directive is addressed to all lenders, but Nigerian banks have a large share of the Gambian market and may be disproportionately affected. So you know, there are 11 banks in The Gambia and four are subsidiaries of Nigerian banking groups: Access Bank, FirstBank, Guaranty Trust Bank and one other. Two of them are among their biggest banks. The CBN has now written to the Nigerian parent banks asking for “a detailed action plan and timeline for achieving compliance”.

UN Human Rights Council Elections for 2027-2029 and the Responsibility to Protect
source: Global Centre for the Responsibility to Protect
text_paragraph_1: Today, 13 October 2026, the UN General Assembly (UNGA) elected Brazil, Burundi, Dominican Republic, Germany, Ghana, Ireland, Japan, Jordan, Kuwait, Nepal, Nigeria, Republic of Moldova, Ukraine, Uruguay and Zambia to the Human Rights Council (HRC) for the 2027-2029 term. With their election, 23 of the Council’s 47 members in 2027 will be “Friends of the Responsibility to Protect (R2P)” – states that have either appointed a Focal Point for R2P and/or joined the Group of Friends of R2P in New York and Geneva.
text_paragraph_2: Following these ‘clean slate’ elections, newly elected members of the HRC have an opportunity to strengthen the Council’s credibility and advance principled leadership in atrocity prevention. Membership in the HRC carries the obligation, set forth in UNGA Resolution 60/251 , to uphold the highest standards of human rights and to fully cooperate with the Council’s mechanisms and procedures. The re-election of Burundi therefore raises serious concerns about the Council’s credibility. Burundi has a documented history of atrocity crimes, and serious human rights violations continue in a climate of widespread impunity. No meaningful structural reforms have been implemented to address long-standing concerns related to human rights, governance, justice and the rule of law. The government of Burundi has also consistently failed to cooperate with the HRC’s mechanisms and has voted against resolutions addressing some of the world’s gravest human rights crises, including in Sudan , Ukraine , South Sudan , Belarus and Eritrea .
text_paragraph_3: Nevertheless, the new composition of the HRC presents a fresh chance to reinforce the Council’s essential role in preventing atrocities and protecting populations at risk, particularly as several members have already demonstrated strong commitments to this goal. For a brief overview of how new HRC members engage with R2P and their status with international legal instruments, see the closing annex in the downloadable PDF version .

The Ministry of Industry says the next stage will concentrate on expanding manufactured exports, adding new productive capacity and modernising the services that support industry, marking an important shift in the programme’s economic purpose. The first phase was largely about getting more out of an industrial base Ethiopia already possessed: reopening factories that had stopped operating, raising utilisation at plants working below capacity, reducing dependence on imported finished goods and creating employment around domestic production. The next phase asks a more demanding question. It is one thing for Ethiopian factories to replace goods that would otherwise have been imported into a domestic market affected by foreign exchange shortages, transport costs and government policies favouring local production. It is considerably harder for the same factories to persuade buyers outside Ethiopia to choose their products over alternatives manufactured in China, India, Turkey, Egypt, Kenya, Vietnam and other competing production centres. If Ethiopia succeeds, “Made in Ethiopia” could evolve from an import substitution programme into something much closer to an export industrialisation strategy.
text_paragraph_3: The scale of the official results explains why the programme is being extended. Reviving 1,115 factories means Ethiopia has attempted to recover productive assets that already contained capital in the form of machinery, factory buildings, established workforces and industrial knowledge rather than relying entirely on building new plants. The reported creation of 1.58 million jobs suggests that the government views industrial expansion not only through the value of manufacturing output but also through its ability to absorb a rapidly growing labour force, while the US$5.96 billion attributed to import substitution points towards another equally important objective: reducing Ethiopia’s persistent demand for foreign exchange. For an economy that has experienced years of hard currency shortages, replacing imported finished products with locally manufactured alternatives can produce benefits even before those factories become internationally competitive, because each product manufactured domestically potentially reduces part of the dollar demand that would otherwise be required to purchase the equivalent product abroad. The economic value of that substitution, however, depends heavily on how much of the production chain has actually moved inside Ethiopia. A factory that assembles imported components can replace a finished import while still requiring substantial foreign currency for machinery, spare parts and intermediate inputs, whereas industries built around Ethiopian agricultural products, minerals, labour and energy can retain a much larger share of value domestically. The US$5.96 billion figure is therefore significant, but the deeper measure of industrial progress will increasingly be how much domestic value Ethiopia adds to each product rather than simply the gross value of goods no longer imported.

His mother’s sudden and unexpected arrest and deportation caused him to miss so much school that he withdrew from his current semester at Kirkwood Community College, though he plans to go back. “I had to step up and at least try to take over her role, which I can’t,” he says. “I’m definitely trying my best with my other siblings, taking care of the house, chores, and stuff like that. text_paragraph_3: Diallo says his mother was detained after dropping off one of his brothers at early morning soccer practice, and then going to her sister’s house to take her to work. text_paragraph_1: For Nyaradzo Auxilia Hoto , one of the most memorable moments of becoming a wildlife ranger was a trip to town. She and her fellow recruits walked through the streets in their new uniforms, on their way to open bank accounts. Soon, they would receive their first salaries. For a woman who had struggled to make ends meet in rural Zimbabwe, it was an extraordinary moment. “We were very proud,” she recalled.
text_paragraph_2: Hoto, 34, grew up in Huyo, a village in Zimbabwe’s Lower Zambezi Valley, where her family depended largely on growing and selling vegetables. Money was scarce, and although she had done well at school, she could not afford to continue her education beyond secondary school. Marriage, she hoped, might offer a better life. Instead, she says, she endured nearly four years with a violent husband before deciding to leave. She returned to her parents’ home with her young daughter and resumed working in the family garden.
text_paragraph_3: Her fortunes changed in 2017, when the International Anti-Poaching Foundation began recruiting local women for Akashinga, a new wildlife protection initiative. Hoto was among 16 women selected from roughly 100 applicants. Many men in her community doubted that women could confront poachers or withstand the demands of ranger work. She went anyway. Within a few years, she had become a ranger sergeant, leading other women on patrol. She later returned to university, graduating in 2023 with a degree in wildlife, ecology and conservation. Today, she works as a biodiversity officer with Akashinga, using data collected by rangers to monitor wildlife and guide conservation decisions. In 2022, she received an International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) International Ranger Award .

MINURSO’s Future: What the Security Council’s Choice May Reveal
text_paragraph_1: On October 31, the United Nations Security Council (UNSC) will vote on whether to renew the UN monitoring mission in Western Sahara, officially known as the UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO). For the past year, the United States has pressed the Security Council to reconsider the mission, raising the possibility of shrinking it, transforming it, or ending it altogether. Yet, despite the growing international support for Morocco’s autonomy plan — under which Western Sahara would gain self-rule but remain under Moroccan sovereignty, rather than become independent — changing MINURSO’s mandate has proven difficult.
text_paragraph_2: The debate over MINURSO’s future raises a larger question about the relationship between the UN mission and the US-led political process. Even as Washington pushes negotiations toward an autonomy-based settlement, the Security Council may still have reasons to preserve MINURSO, the institution originally created to organize a referendum on the territory’s future. Three alternatives have been under consideration: ending the mission, scaling it back to monitoring, or transforming it to implement autonomy. Each faces obstacles, raising the possibility that after a year of pressure, MINURSO may survive unchanged.
text_paragraph_3: The Western Sahara is a former Spanish colony claimed by both Morocco and the Polisario Front, an Algeria-backed Sahrawi political movement that seeks independence. Efforts to resolve the decades-long conflict between the two sides, which dates back to 1975, have centered on the principle of self-determination, initially tied to a referendum under the UN 1991 Settlement Plan. MINURSO was established that year to prepare for the referendum and monitor the cease-fire as an impartial UN presence on both sides of the berm, a fortified barrier built by Morocco to contain insurgent incursions.
